clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant polyglutamine disorder combining ataxia, chorea, dementia, myoclonus and epilepsy in variable proportions
Caused by a CAG repeat expansion in ATN1 encoding atrophin-1
Phenotype is strongly age-dependent: juvenile-onset disease resembles a progressive myoclonic epilepsy, whereas adult-onset disease resembles a Huntington-like ataxia-chorea-dementia syndrome
Reported most commonly in Japanese populations, though it occurs worldwide (the Haw River kindred being a well-known example)
Shows marked anticipation, particularly with paternal transmission, so children may be far more severely affected than the parent
MRI reveals cerebellar and brainstem atrophy, often with cerebral white-matter change
Seizures and myoclonus are prominent in early-onset cases and demand active management
Care is supportive and symptomatic, addressing seizures, movement disorder, mood and cognition
reference.pathophysiology: DRPLA results from expansion of a CAG trinucleotide repeat in ATN1, yielding an atrophin-1 protein with an elongated polyglutamine tract. The mutant protein is cleaved and accumulates in neuronal nuclei as intranuclear inclusions, disrupting transcriptional regulation and other cellular processes through a toxic gain-of-function. Neurodegeneration characteristically affects the dentatorubral and pallidoluysian systems, alongside the cerebellum, cerebral cortex and white matter, producing the mixed ataxic, choreic, myoclonic, epileptic and cognitive phenotype. The repeat is highly unstable across generations, especially paternally, giving pronounced anticipation and a shift toward the severe juvenile phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Huntington disease and Huntington disease-like disorders
SCA17 and other polyglutamine spinocerebellar ataxias
Mitochondrial disorders with ataxia, epilepsy and myoclonus
Wilson disease and other treatable movement disorders
additionalInvestigations: EEG to characterise seizures and myoclonus, particularly in young patients
MRI brain assessing cerebellar, brainstem and cerebral white-matter change
Huntington disease testing when the adult phenotype is Huntington-like and ATN1 is negative
Screening for treatable metabolic mimics when appropriate
redFlags: Status epilepticus or frequent drop attacks in juvenile-onset disease
Rapid cognitive and motor deterioration in a child suggesting a large expansion
Pronounced anticipation in a pedigree indicating high risk of severe disease in offspring
reference.prognosis: DRPLA is progressive and ultimately fatal; juvenile-onset disease advances rapidly with early severe disability, whereas adult-onset disease progresses more slowly over years to a couple of decades. Prognosis worsens with larger repeat expansions and earlier onset.
pitfalls: Diagnosing an unclassified progressive myoclonic epilepsy in a child without considering DRPLA
Testing only for Huntington disease in adult-onset chorea-dementia and missing DRPLA
Underestimating anticipation and paternal transmission risk when counselling families
Overlooking the epilepsy and myoclonus that often drive early morbidity
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No curative or disease-modifying treatment is available; management is symptomatic and supportive
Use anticonvulsants such as valproate, levetiracetam and benzodiazepines to control seizures and myoclonus, particularly in the juvenile progressive myoclonic epilepsy phenotype
Treat chorea with dopamine-depleting or antidopaminergic agents and manage ataxia and parkinsonism symptomatically
Address dementia and psychiatric symptoms with appropriate pharmacological and psychosocial support
Provide multidisciplinary rehabilitation including physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy, with attention to swallowing safety and nutrition
Introduce palliative care as disability progresses
Offer genetic counselling for the autosomal dominant CAG-repeat expansion, explaining anticipation and the greater severity with paternal transmission
